Tilkhos (Capoeta gracilis) reaches a maximum standard length of 21.17 centimeters [Li = 21.17 centimeters] according to recent morphometric surveys conducted in the upper Kura River basin, though some ichthyological databases report a larger ultimate total length of 35 centimeters for this cyprinid. The species exhibits a comparatively moderate body size relative to other members of the genus Capoeta, which often attain greater asymptotic dimensions in larger river systems. Regional variation in growth trajectories may reflect differences in food availability and thermal regimes across the species’ fragmented montane distribution. The ultimate length was derived from a sample of older individuals collected during spawning runs, and it likely represents the upper bound of somatic growth under natural conditions. Factors such as density-dependent competition and seasonal resource pulses probably contribute to the observed variability in maximum size among populations. Further investigation into age-at-length relationships would clarify whether the 21.17 centimeters figure represents a true asymptotic plateau or a sampling artefact from size-selective mortality.

Female Tilkhos attain puberty at a fork length of 11.82 centimeters [Lp = 11.82 centimeters], a size that corresponds broadly with the onset of vitellogenesis and the first appearance of mature oocytes in histological examinations. This length at sexual maturation is modest compared to other cyprinids in the region, where related species often require a larger body size before gonadal recrudescence begins. The transition to reproductive maturity appears closely tied to somatic growth rates, with individuals in more productive reaches reaching the pubertal threshold more quickly than those in oligotrophic headwaters. Seasonal cues, particularly photoperiod and spring temperature increases, likely synchronise the final stages of gametogenesis once the critical 11.82 centimeters fork length has been attained. Population-level variation in this pubertal length may also reflect genotype-by-environment interactions, with cooler streams selecting for a slightly larger size at maturity as a bet-hedging strategy against unpredictable spawning seasons.

Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae of Tilkhos have a wet weight at birth of 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams], a value derived from the measured egg diameter of approximately 1.7 millimeters. This minute birth mass places the species among the smaller propagule producers within the Capoeta lineage, consistent with an overall life-history strategy that favours high fecundity at the expense of per-offspring investment. The egg size itself determines the initial larval provisioning, and the 0.0026 grams of wet tissue reflects the cytoplasmic volume available to support the lecithotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding. Endotrophic larvae rely entirely on this yolk reserve during the first days post-eclosion, during which time the mouth remains closed and the larvae remain largely sessile. The small birth mass imposes constraints on early survival, as larvae must locate suitable planktonic prey within a narrow window following yolk-sac resorption to avoid starvation-induced mortality. Field observations indicate that larvae dispersing into productive stream reaches experience higher survival rates, presumably because prey densities are sufficient to bridge the trophic transition.

When maintained at a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum reproductive output of female Tilkhos reaches a theoretical upper limit estimated from daily egg production under controlled conditions. This species exhibits a high fecundity for a small-bodied cyprinid: females produce an average of 257 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 257 eggs per clutch] per spawning event, and under optimal thermal conditions can spawn approximately 365 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 times per year], reflecting a nearly continuous breeding strategy during the active season. The entire annual reproductive output of approximately 93860 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 93860 eggs per year] highlights the capacity for substantial reproductive investment, a life-history adaptation to unpredictable egg and larval survivorship in the species' native torrential habitats. The 18 °C temperature is critical for maintaining enzymatic pathways involved in oocyte maturation and hormonal cycling, and deviations from this regime can reduce both clutch size and spawning intervals. Actual field rates are often lower due to energetic constraints and environmental stochasticity.

Under steady thermal conditions of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for Tilkhos is 4 years [am = 4 years], a relatively compressed longevity that aligns with the species’ fast-paced life history and high reproductive allocation. This lifespan of 1460 days [am = 1460 days] was documented in a mark-recapture study spanning multiple cohorts in the Kura River system, where the oldest individuals recovered were four-year-old adults exhibiting signs of gonadal senescence at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. The relatively short maximum lifespan is typical of small-bodied cyprinids inhabiting dynamic lotic environments, where predation pressure and seasonal floods impose high extrinsic mortality rates. Physiological age-related changes, including reduced condition factor and lower gonadosomatic indices, become apparent by the third year, suggesting that reproductive value peaks earlier in life. The 4-year longevity figure also implies that most individuals participate in only two or three spawning seasons, making each annual breeding event critical for population persistence. Comparative life-table analyses indicate that populations experiencing lower thermal regimes may exhibit slightly extended lifespans, though the 18 °C baseline appears to define the species’ fundamental demographic boundary under optimal laboratory conditions.
